extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, crisis communicators, and scholars/educators evaluating crisis messages
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing and assessing corporate crisis-response messages using Benoit's theory of image restoration discourse; covers strategy typology, audience analysis, preparation, and practical recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack components: responsibility and offensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: An attack prompting image repair has two components: (1) the accused is held responsible for an action, and (2) that act is considered offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility can include acts performed, ordered, encouraged, facilitated, permitted, omissions, or poorly performed acts. Whether an act is offensive depends on salient audience perception. Importantly, perceptions (what the audience believes) matter more than objective reality; a firm’s image is at risk if relevant audiences believe the firm is responsible or that the act is offensive. Thus diagnosis of perceived responsibility and offensiveness is the first step in evaluating or crafting responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and prioritize salient audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations often face multiple audiences (e.g., citizens, regulators, stockholders, employees, pressure groups, politicians) whose interests diverge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The crisis communicator must identify the most important audience(s) and prioritize responses accordingly. Messages should be tailored to the concerns of each salient audience, possibly using different messages for different groups, but avoid developing contradictory messages. Example: regulators care about law compliance; stockholders about profits; environmentalists about ecological harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial (image restoration strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject that the offensive act occurred, that the firm performed it, or that it was harmful to anyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denial can be direct (declare allegations false) or include shifting blame (argue another party is responsible). Example: Coca‑Cola's direct denial of Pepsi's pricing charge; Exxon blaming officials/Coast Guard for cleanup delay. Anti-pattern: false denials that later prove untrue can severely damage credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evasion of responsibility (image restoration strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce or reject culpability by portraying the act as excused or beyond firm control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four variants: (a) Provocation — claim the act was a reasonable response to another's offensive act; (b) Defeasibility — allege lack of information or control (e.g., 'I was never told'); (c) Accident — claim the act was inadvertent; (d) Good intentions — stress benevolent motives. Examples: moving a plant because of law changes (provocation); missed meeting because not told (defeasibility); Sears calling mistakes 'inadvertent' (accident); stressing long history of good intent. Risks: audience may not accept excuses if evidence contradicts them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce offensiveness (image restoration strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to lessen the perceived offensiveness of the attributed act through reframing or compensatory moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Six versions described: (1) Bolstering — emphasize positive traits or past good acts to offset negativity; (2) Minimization — downplay the seriousness of harm; (3) Differentiation — distinguish the act from more offensive acts; (4) Transcendence — place the act in a more favorable, often higher-order context (e.g., greater good); (5) Attack the accuser — discredit or counter-attack critics; (6) Compensation — apologize and offer reparations acceptable to victims. Examples: Exxon's statements aimed to bolster; Sears characterized repairs as preventative maintenance (differentiation); offering free passes to rebuffed moviegoers (compensation). Anti-patterns: minimization can backfire if it seems to trivialize harm; attacking accusers risks escalating conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective action (image restoration strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Promise and undertake steps to repair the damage and prevent recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrective action can restore the previous state and/or commit to preventing future occurrences. Effective responses describe specific remediation steps and investments (e.g., AT&T's facility examinations and increased spending). Important: promises must be credible and followed by action — unfulfilled corrective claims can backfire and further damage credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortification (apology) (image restoration strategy)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apology can restore image but may invite legal consequences (e.g., lawsuits). Use when admitting fault is appropriate and likely to restore trust; weigh moral/PR benefits against legal risks. Example: AT&T offered apology as part of its response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation: crisis contingency planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Before crises, organizations should prepare contingency plans and designate responsibility for crisis response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign a responsible person or team, anticipate plausible crises for the organization (e.g., airlines plan for crashes; restaurants for food‑poisoning), review and update plans periodically, and practice implementation. Fast, well-prepared responses (e.g., Tylenol) can reduce missteps; slow or uncoordinated reactions (e.g., Exxon) can undermine repair efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the crisis and accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a crisis occurs, clearly determine the nature of the accusations and the perceived severity of the offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurately diagnose what is being alleged and how serious audiences perceive the offense to be; tailor the response strategy to fit the nature and severity. Misdiagnosis can lead to inappropriate or counterproductive messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding whether to respond and how to reshape attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all accusations require response; choices include redefining the attack, refocusing attention, or declining to engage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accusations are not important to the salient audience(s) or are unlikely to gain traction, a firm may avoid responding. Alternatives include redefining the attack or refocusing public attention on other issues. If a charge becomes important or is repeated, the firm may be forced to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamentals of persuasive credibility: avoid false claims and support assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Image restoration is persuasive discourse; general persuasion rules apply: do not make false claims, provide adequate support, develop themes, and avoid arguments that may backfire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self‑serving or unsupported claims damage credibility (e.g., Exxon's self‑serving cleanup claims undermined credibility when contradicted by reports). Develop consistent themes across communications. Anti-pattern: making claims that conflict with known facts or other statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a clearly identified, prominent spokesperson
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and use an effective and credible spokesperson to deliver responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clearly identified and prominent company spokesperson can lend credibility and clarity (e.g., Coke used a prominent company spokesperson effectively), whereas an ineffectual choice (e.g., an outside lawyer) can undermine the message. Spokesperson selection should consider audience trust and perceived legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit fault when at fault (weigh against litigation risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the firm is actually at fault, admitting responsibility promptly can aid image restoration, but may conflict with legal risk avoidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt admission can be morally appropriate and restore trust; false denials that are later disproven harm credibility. The firm must balance PR benefits of admission against potential legal exposure. Examples: AT&T eventually accepted responsibility and this likely helped restore image; Union Carbide perhaps should have accepted some responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defeasibility and identifying external causes
rubrics_metrics.description: If factors beyond one's control caused the offense, emphasizing these can alleviate responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that lack of information, poor conditions, or external factors contributed to or caused the problem (e.g., poor ocean conditions hindering cleanup). Use when credible; fabricating external causes risks further damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate concrete corrective and preventive plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly report plans to correct the problem and to prevent recurrence as part of image repair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences want to know what will be done to fix the harm and prevent repeats. Detailed, believable plans (with timelines, investments, actions) can reassure stakeholders. Example: Tylenol introduced tamper‑resistant packaging; AT&T described plans for increased reliability. Risk: failing to implement promised measures damages credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of minimization and beware backlash
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimizing the severity of the offense may not improve image and can provoke backlash if perceived as dismissive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to downplay serious problems can look feeble or deceptive (e.g., Exxon's minimization efforts may have been counterproductive). Use minimization cautiously and only when credible evidence supports the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple consistent strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple image restoration strategies can be used together when consistent and complementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies like bolstering, compensation, and corrective action can reinforce each other (e.g., Union Carbide combined alleviation plans with bolstering). Ensure that combined strategies do not contradict one another; inconsistency undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of persuasion and the role of time
rubrics_metrics.description: There are limits to what persuasive communication can achieve; sometimes waiting until public attention fades is the only option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some crises (e.g., major environmental disasters), little immediate communication can fully restore image; organizations may need to accept limited short‑term repair and rely on time and long‑term actions. Manage expectations accordingly.
